column4: The section explicitly says the resurrection passage asks about crops as well as fire; this opens the paired question about what people cultivate, placing human use of provision beside the fire they kindle.
This is the crop question the section names: people sow, but God asks whether they make it grow or He does, paralleling the distinction between kindling fire and creating its source.
In the crop passage the section identifies, God says He could make the harvest dry debris; the possible loss of what people cultivate extends the section’s concern with fire’s ash and what remains.
This continues the crop question named by the section: the people’s response to a ruined harvest shows their dependence on provision rather than authorship of it.
The crop passage continues with the people saying they have been deprived; this is their response to the loss whose possibility 56:65 establishes, within the provision sequence the section names.
The section explicitly names the water question that precedes its fire question; this begins the parallel challenge about the source of a daily provision.
This continues the water question the section names, asking whether people send down what they drink or God does; it parallels the distinction between using a provision and creating it.
The water sequence the section names ends with God’s power to make it bitter and a question about gratitude, preparing the same recognition of divine provision that surrounds the fire question.
After the section’s cited fire is called a reminder and provision in 56:73, this neighboring ayah commands glorifying the Lord; it supplies the worshipful response to the created fire’s reminder.

The fire encounter’s speech continues from the guidance Moses seeks in 20:10: this ayah says the Hour is coming and each soul is recompensed for its striving, meeting the section’s dictionary sense of a kindled undertaking reaching its aim.

The same speech warns Moses not to be turned aside by someone who rejects the Hour and follows desire; it gives a specific form of the section’s contrast between a purposeful spark and the spark of misguidance.

The section defines مصباح through the dictionary form سراج; this verse says the lowest heaven is adorned with “مصابيح” and guarded, giving the Quranic lamp a protective, enduring role unlike useless sparks in the air.

The section calls sparks flying through the air useless; this ayah names the sky’s “مصابيح” and says they are made as missiles against devils, a specific contrast between airborne fire that has no use and lights given a purpose.
The section mentions Moses’ “شهاب قبس” and sparks flying in air; here a “شهاب ثاقب” pursues a listener in the heavens, turning a similar aerial flame into a purposeful guard.
The section mentions the burning brand “شهاب قبس”; this ayah’s “شهاب مبين” follows one who steals a hearing, a Quranic use of the same flame-word for a directed act rather than useless sparks.
This opens the passage about the heavens being filled with guards and flames, the setting for the next ayah’s waiting “شهابا”; it broadens the section’s airborne-fire image to guarded skies.
Continuing 72:8, this says a listener now finds a “شهابا رصدا”; alongside the section’s “شهاب قبس” and useless flying sparks, it depicts an airborne flame with a specific purpose.
The section describes a hard strike on stone releasing sparks; here Moses strikes a stone by God’s command and water springs out, a specific reversal in what a blow on stone releases.
This retelling likewise has Moses strike a stone, but twelve springs flow from it; it gives a second Quranic outcome for the stone-strike scene, water rather than the section’s sparks.

The section’s fire-making tool is iron struck against stone; here iron is worked until it is heated like fire and molten metal is poured over it. The link is the iron-and-fire craft, though this ayah builds a barrier rather than making a spark.
The section presents fire as an ignition whose output may be useful or futile; here God commands the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham, a specific reversal of fire’s ordinary burning effect.

The section’s dictionary branch says sun or fire can change an object’s color; “لواحة للبشر” is commonly read as Saqar scorching or blackening human skin, though the word has interpretive range, giving a destructive counterpart to that color-changing branch.
The section contrasts a brief spark with morning light; this asks who could bring light if God made the night continuous, directly marking the dependence of people in darkness on real light.
The paired question asks who could bring night for rest if God made day continuous; it sets the section’s morning light within the reciprocal night-and-day boundary.
The section develops morning as daylight that displaces darkness; this oath names “الفجر,” dawn itself, another direct Quranic formulation of the light-boundary image.

The section connects 100:8’s intense love of “good” with worldly wealth; this ayah describes the wealth-collector who amasses and counts it, giving a concrete form to that attachment before the fire passage in 104:6-7.

The section ties an unhelpful horse-spark to the neighboring love of wealth; in the passage about the wealth-collector, this is “نار الله الموقدة,” a kindled fire with real consequence rather than a spark that benefits no one.
This continues 104:6 by saying the kindled fire rises over hearts; next to the section’s wealth-love and useless “hubabib” sparks, it gives that fire-word a consequential, inward counterpart.
